hist-em-02-c1.text: Mark Cartwright (2021). Ferdinand Magellan. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-02-c1.quote: but da Gama did round the Cape of Good Hope and cross the Indian Ocean to reach India in 1498.
hist-em-02-c1.claim: Vasco da Gama reached India via the Cape of Good Hope in 1498, opening a direct sea route to the spice trade.

hist-em-02-c2.text: John Horgan (2022). Columbian Exchange. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-02-c2.quote: The exchange began in the aftermath of Christopher Columbus' voyages in 1492, later accelerating with the European colonization of the Americas.
hist-em-02-c2.claim: Columbus's arrival in 1492 initiated the Columbian Exchange: a biological revolution that permanently altered both hemispheres.

hist-em-03-c1.text: Joshua J. Mark (2022). John Calvin. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-03-c1.quote: Luther's central argument was that scripture alone was the source of truth and an individual was justified by faith in God alone, not by works nor by following the teachings of the Catholic Church.
hist-em-03-c1.claim: Luther argued that salvation came through faith alone (sola fide), not works or Church intercession.

hist-em-07-c1.text: John Horgan (2022). Columbian Exchange. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-07-c1.quote: Europe transformed those raw materials into finished goods which were traded to Africa and the Americas, while Africa supplied slaves to fulfill labor needs in the New World.
hist-em-07-c1.claim: The Atlantic trade developed into roughly triangular patterns: manufactured goods (cloth, weapons, alcohol) from Europe to Africa; enslaved Africans across the Middle Passage to the Americas;

hist-em-07-c1.text: John Horgan (2022). Columbian Exchange. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-07-c1.quote: in which the Americas supplied the Old World with raw materials
hist-em-07-c1.claim: raw materials and crops (sugar, tobacco, cotton, rum) from the Americas back to Europe.

hist-em-01-c1.text: Mark Cartwright (2020). Petrarch. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-01-c1.quote: Consequently, Petrarch is often cited as the founder of humanism.
hist-em-01-c1.claim: Humanist scholars like Petrarch (1304–1374), often called the 'first humanist', turned away from medieval theology and toward ancient Roman and Greek texts.

hist-em-01-c2.text: Mark Cartwright (2020). Leonardo da Vinci. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-01-c2.quote: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519) was an Italian Renaissance artist, architect, engineer, and scientist.
hist-em-01-c2.claim: Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was the Renaissance ideal in one person: painter, sculptor, architect, engineer, anatomist, and inventor.

hist-em-01-c2.text: Mark Cartwright (2020). Michelangelo. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-01-c2.quote: His most celebrated works, from a breathtaking portfolio of masterpieces, include the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome and the giant marble statue of David, which resides in the Galleria dell'Accademia of Florence.
hist-em-01-c2.claim: Michelangelo (1475–1564) painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508–1512) and sculpted David.

hist-em-01-c3.text: Joshua J. Mark (2021). Martin Luther. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-01-c3.quote: Luther's theses were translated by his followers into German, printed, and disseminated, sparking widespread challenges to ecclesiastical authority in Germany and, translated and spread further, in England, France, and other regions.
hist-em-01-c3.claim: When Martin Luther nailed his 95 Theses in 1517, they were printed and circulated across Germany within weeks.

hist-em-04-c1.text: J J O'Connor, E F Robertson. Nicolaus Copernicus - Biography. MacTutor History of Mathematics.
hist-em-04-c1.quote: A full account of Copernicus's theory was apparently slow to reach a state in which he wished to see it published, and this did not happen until the very end of Copernicus's life when he published his life's work under the title De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (Nuremberg, 1543).
hist-em-04-c1.claim: Nicolaus Copernicus proposed in 1543 that the Earth orbits the Sun (heliocentrism), challenging both Church doctrine and Aristotelian physics.

hist-em-04-c1.text: J J O'Connor, E F Robertson. Galileo Galilei - Biography. MacTutor History of Mathematics.
hist-em-04-c1.quote: Found guilty, Galileo was condemned to lifelong imprisonment, but the sentence was carried out somewhat sympathetically and it amounted to house arrest rather than a prison sentence.
hist-em-04-c1.claim: His championing of Copernicus led to his trial by the Inquisition (1633) and house arrest for the rest of his life.

hist-em-04-c3.text: Kaya Şahin (2023). Suleiman the Magnificent. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-04-c3.quote: Hailed as a skilled military commander, a just ruler, and a divinely anointed monarch during his lifetime, his realm extended from Hungary to Iran, and from Crimea to North Africa and the Indian Ocean.
hist-em-04-c3.claim: The Ottoman Empire at its height under Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520–1566) stretched from Hungary to Arabia, and from North Africa to Persia.

hist-em-04-c3.text: Mark Cartwright (2019). The Seven Voyages of Zheng He. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-04-c3.quote: Between 1405 and 1433 CE Zheng He commanded huge fleets loaded with trade goods and high-value gifts to such far-flung places as Hormuz in the Persian Gulf and Mogadishu in East Africa.
hist-em-04-c3.claim: In China, the Ming Dynasty (1368–1644) sponsored the extraordinary naval expeditions of Zheng He (1405–1433), whose treasure ships visited Southeast Asia, India, Arabia, and the East African coast

hist-em-05-c1.text: Alex Tuckness (2005). Locke’s Political Philosophy. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
hist-em-05-c1.quote: Since governments exist by the consent of the people in order to protect the rights of the people and promote the public good, governments that fail to do so can be resisted and replaced with new governments.
hist-em-05-c1.claim: John Locke (1632–1704) argued that governments derive authority from the consent of the governed, and that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property.

hist-em-05-c3.text: Harrison W. Mark (2022). Storming of the Bastille. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-05-c3.quote: On 14 July 1789, the Bastille, a fortress and political prison symbolizing the oppressiveness of France’s Ancien Régime was attacked by a crowd mainly consisting of sans-culottes, or lower classes.
hist-em-05-c3.claim: The storming of the Bastille (July 14, 1789) symbolized the fall of the Old Regime.

hist-em-05-c3.text: Harrison W. Mark (2022). Reign of Terror. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-05-c3.quote: 16,594 of these 'suspects' were formally executed after a trial, while around 10,000 died in prison, and thousands more were killed in various massacres staged across France.
hist-em-05-c3.claim: The Revolution devoured itself: the Reign of Terror (1793–1794) under Robespierre saw thousands guillotined.

hist-em-06-c1.text: Joshua J. Mark (2021). Salem Witch Trials. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-06-c1.quote: The Salem Witch Trials were a series of legal proceedings in Salem, Massachusetts in 1692-1693 resulting in the deaths of 20 innocent people accused of witchcraft and the vilification of over 200 others
hist-em-06-c1.claim: The Salem witch trials (1692, Massachusetts) were smaller in scale.

hist-em-06-c2.text: Newton and Alchemy. The Chymistry of Isaac Newton, Indiana University.
hist-em-06-c2.quote: In that year the venerable auction house of Sotheby's released a catalogue describing three hundred twenty-nine lots of Newton's manuscripts, mostly in his own handwriting, of which over a third were filled with content that was undeniably alchemical.
hist-em-06-c2.claim: Newton spent enormous time on alchemy.

hist-em-08-c1.text: Harrison W. Mark (2026). Louis XIV of France: The Sun King. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-08-c1.quote: Known as Le Roi Soleil ('the Sun King'), he fervently believed in the concept of the 'divine right' of kings and is remembered for ruling as an absolute monarch.
hist-em-08-c1.claim: Louis XIV of France (1643-1715, the 'Sun King') is the model

hist-em-08-c2.text: Mark Cartwright (2021). Charles I of England. World History Encyclopedia.
hist-em-08-c2.quote: Charles I was executed on 30 January 1649.
hist-em-08-c2.claim: The English Civil War (1642-51) executed King Charles I; the Glorious Revolution (1688) deposed James II for William III.

hist-em-08-c3.text: Sharon A. Lloyd, Susanne Sreedhar (2002). Hobbes’s Moral and Political Philosophy. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
hist-em-08-c3.quote: And the life of man, solitary, poore, nasty, brutish, and short.
hist-em-08-c3.claim: Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) defended strong sovereign authority, without which life is 'nasty, brutish, and short'.
